title: Session 1 — Participant 4 User + Claude Behavior Graphs
goal: Organize a literature review for an academic study about first-time ultramarathon experiences and identify potential instrumentation.

Step 1.step_name: Find literature related to first-time ultramarathon experiences
Step 1.step_action: Ask Claude to provide information on what literature exists regarding first-time ultramarathon experiences

nodes.label: Ask for literature bridging ECT and self-efficacy
nodes.detail: Sends a request to find literature that informs what is already known about expectation-confirmation theory and self-efficacy in runners or other extreme physical sports, to justify asking the research question.

nodes.label: Generate bridging literature justifying the study
nodes.detail: Identifies a PhD thesis (Anstiss) on the self-efficacy construct in endurance sport as the key bridging source, plus supporting literature: ESSES development papers, a Hazelwood & Burke ultra-endurance triathlon study, and a HURT100 mental-toughness study.

nodes.label: Read the bridging literature and finish the session.
nodes.detail: Begins reading through the bridging-literature response; the last two minutes of the recording show no further scrolling, typing, or clicking, and the video cuts off mid-read with no outline-synthesis step shown on screen.

Step 2.step_name: Generate a research question related to first-time experiences of ultrarunners
Step 2.step_action: Ask Claude to generate ideas for areas of study related to various aspects of this area. Ask Claude to base these directions of study on recommendations for further research. Ask Claude to propose 5 different research questions related to this topic.

nodes.label: Compose a message to Claude that they're moving from literature search toward research-question generation
nodes.detail: Starts typing a message to Claude signaling they're moving on from the literature search toward generating a research question.

nodes.label: Generate candidate research questions
nodes.detail: Proposes a broad/exploratory research question and a second question explicitly framed through expectation-disconfirmation theory, tying the questions back to the ECT literature discussed earlier.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to re-identify the trail-running IPA study
nodes.detail: Asks Claude, as an aside, what the trail-running IPA study referenced earlier in the conversation actually is; this exact question recurs later in the same segment.

nodes.label: Re-identify the trail-running IPA study
nodes.detail: Reminds them it is 'Like Nothing I've Seen Before' on PMC, restating its key details; answers the identical question again later in the segment.

nodes.label: Review remaining research question options and begin logging them and rename the theory note to Expectation (Dis)Confirmation Theory
nodes.detail: Reads the narrower, mechanism-focused RQ option, then opens the scratchpad to start a 'Possible Research Questions' list, logging the first candidate question.

nodes.label: Review design considerations and log a design note for pre/post data collection approach
nodes.detail: Reads Claude's closing considerations on timing of data collection and what counts as 'first-time,' then adds a 'Design:' heading noting a prospective pre/post data-collection approach.

nodes.label: Review Claude's answer about the trail-running IPA study
nodes.detail: Check out Claude's answer on 'Like Nothing I've Seen Before'

Step 3.step_name: Organize a theoretical framework for an academic study about first-time ultramarathon experiences.
Step 3.step_action: Ask Claude to relate this topic to frameworks related to psychology, motivation, and public health. Ask Claude to integrate these frameworks and also organize a sequence of literature topics to lead to the specific topic, population, and research question

nodes.label: Ask Claude to define outcomes of interest
nodes.detail: Sends a message asking Claude to address both the immediate expectation-reality gap and the longer-term implications of the ultramarathon experience.

nodes.label: Generate a two-layer outcomes framework
nodes.detail: Defines 'Layer 1' (the immediate expectation-reality gap across physical, emotional, cognitive, and social domains) and 'Layer 2' (longer-term outcomes: intent to continue, self-concept, recalibration, meaning-making, identity), plus a unifying descriptive-vs-relational framing.

nodes.label: Transcribe the Layer 1 expectation-gap domains
nodes.detail: Adds a 'Short-term experience: expected vs actual' section to the scratchpad, logging the physical, emotional, cognitive, and social/environmental sub-domains Claude proposed.

nodes.label: Transcribe Layer 2 and the unifying framework
nodes.detail: Logs the longer-term outcome variables (intent to continue, self-efficacy/self-concept, re-calibration, meaning-making, identity-labeling) and then the unifying 'Potential framework' heading with Claude's descriptive-aim/relational-aim quote.

Step 4.step_name: Identify possible instrumentation for further investigation in studying experiences of first-time ultramarathoners
Step 4.step_action: Ask Claude for instrumentation regarding expectation vs. experience.

nodes.label: Send a request for instrumentation ideas
nodes.detail: Finishes and sends them message asking what kinds of instruments would measure both expectation-disconfirmation and self-efficacy for this study.

nodes.label: Recommend validated self-efficacy scales
nodes.detail: Identifies the Endurance Sport Self-Efficacy Scale (ESSES), Barrier Self-Efficacy Scale, and Physical Self-Efficacy Scale, noting no validated ECT-based instrument exists for endurance sport.

nodes.label: Review and open the link from Claude's answer about potential instrument and log it
nodes.detail: Logs a scale into the scratchpad's new 'Potential instruments' list and confirms its details on an external journal site; this verify-and-log pattern recurs once more later in the segment with a different source.
nodes.softwares: Claude, Microsoft Word, web browser (ScienceDirect, PLOS ONE)

nodes.label: Review and transcribe the ECT measurement structure
nodes.detail: Reads Claude's Oliver-(1980)-based four-part measurement template (pre-experience expectations, perceived performance, disconfirmation, satisfaction) and copies it into the instrument outline.

nodes.label: Ask for clarification from Claude on an instrument-design point
nodes.detail: Questions whether the drafted expectation/experience item pairs actually come from ESSES or are being invented; pushes back again later in the segment when frustrated by an over-long detour into the Oliver scoring method.

nodes.label: Clarifies the instrument approach
nodes.detail: Clarifies the item pairs are researcher-constructed rather than drawn from ESSES; later apologizes for the frustrating detour and redrafts the items using the direct-disconfirmation approach they chose.

nodes.label: Review Claude's clarification and weigh design options
nodes.detail: Logs Claude's clarification into the scratchpad and weighs the three implied paths forward (researcher-developed measure, anchoring to existing frameworks, or qualitative-only).

nodes.label: Express confusion, scroll up and down on Claude's answer, and finally request concrete item pairs
nodes.detail: Admits they are getting a little lost in the theoretical options and asks Claude directly to draft ultrarunning-specific expectation-vs-experience item pairs.

nodes.label: Draft item pairs and compare scoring approaches
nodes.detail: Generates matched item pairs across six domains (physical, pacing/effort, emotional, cognitive, social, self-concept) and compares subtractive/computed disconfirmation (Oliver, 1980) versus direct/subjective disconfirmation (Tse & Wilton, 1988), recommending the latter, plus a justification plan.

nodes.label: Read Claude's answer on the item pairs and scoring comparison and revise notes by adding new papers from Claude
nodes.detail: Reviews the item pairs and scoring comparison, then rewrites an earlier annotation to correctly describe the Tse & Wilton direct-disconfirmation option, adding an 'Instrument justification' heading.

nodes.label: Work on instrument justification as suggested by Claude
nodes.detail: Copies the six domain-specific direct-disconfirmation item pairs and practical notes (single post-race measurement point, optional pre-race checklist) into a new 'Instrument idea flesh-out' section.

nodes.label: Review the outline and pivot back toward literature
nodes.detail: Scrolls back through the scratchpad's earlier sections, then begins typing a message asking to return to finding literature that justifies the research question.

Step 1.step_name: Find literature related to first-time ultramarathon experiences
Step 1.step_action: Ask Claude to provide information on what literature exists regarding first-time ultramarathon experiences

3 academic studies with findings related to this interest area

ratings.output_quality_reason: Finding relevant literature seems to be difficult for AI, it finds articles that are off-target and often describes a particular article but then links a different one. I really only got one on-target article that I was looking for in today’s session, although I typed several others into my list today to look up later. I didn’t look those up now for time reasons. I’ve noticed this before, AI is really no better (and often worse) than a search engine for literature searching. I think it’s because it can’t read my mind in terms of what I’m looking for in articles. I can try and prompt it, but ultimately I’m making qualitative judgements about them that AI can’t know.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: I only got one on-target article from today’s session, although I do have several more to look up. It’s hard to immediately assess this based on the session because I have to look up the articles and go over them separately, which takes some time.

Step 2.step_name: Generate a research question related to first-time experiences of ultrarunners
Step 2.step_action: Ask Claude to generate ideas for areas of study related to various aspects of this area. Ask Claude to base these directions of study on recommendations for further research. Ask Claude to propose 5 different research questions related to this topic.
Step 2.output: 5 different research questions, along with a justification for each based on recommendations for further research in previous literature.
rubrics: 5 different research questions related to the topic of first-time experiences of ultrarunners
Questions are based on previous findings, as well as recommendations for future research

ratings.output_quality_reason: I don’t think I’m ready for a research question yet, I think I should have built some of the theoretical framework first and then asked this prompt later. This is something I’m going to have to come back to, and adjust the research question to match the variable outputs that we created in the later prompts. The question is alright, but it’s too broad and will need to be honed.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: Technically, it gave me some research questions. However, I think I would have gotten better responses and more usable questions if I had saved this step for later in the conversation when it had some more context.

Step 3.step_name: Organize a theoretical framework for an academic study about first-time ultramarathon experiences.
Step 3.step_action: Ask Claude to relate this topic to frameworks related to psychology, motivation, and public health. Ask Claude to integrate these frameworks and also organize a sequence of literature topics to lead to the specific topic, population, and research question
Step 3.output: A few different frameworks related to studying the first time ultramarathon experiences, that shape the literature review and purpose of an academic paper.
rubrics: 2 different framework outlines that might be used to justify a research question about first-time ultramarathon experiences
frameworks contain one theory/model to base potential hypothesis on

ratings.output_quality_reason: I had never heard of the ECT theory before, but I think it fits well. The AI did a good job of hanging onto that theory and incorporating it into my questions. This step probably saved me hours that normally would have been spent trying to figure this out on my own.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: It came up with 2 different theoretical bases for this study, one of which I’d never heard of, but that I preliminarily feel very comfortable moving forward with. This is one of the harder parts of formulating a research paper, and I felt that Claude did exceptionally well with this.

Step 4.step_name: Identify possible instrumentation for further investigation in studying experiences of first-time ultramarathoners
Step 4.step_action: Ask Claude for instrumentation regarding expectation vs. experience.
Step 4.output: A few ideas for instruments regarding potential research questions
rubrics: 3 instrumentation possibilities for measuring various aspects of expectation vs. experiences

ratings.output_quality_reason: THis is another aspect of academic paper-writing that I feel is very difficult and cumbersome. I still feel like this aspect will take quite a bit more work, but Claude got a good start on it.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: I feel like there is alot of work between the ideas from the output today and an actual instrument. AI comes up with good ideas and a good general description, but there are alot of details to finalize to make sure that the answers generated from the instrument are analyze-able, and match the desired outputs in the hypotheses. It’s easy to come up with general questions, but when you’re finalizing it, you have to be very precise with the instrument questions, or the answers won’t match the research questions or the needed statistical analysis.

Step 5.output: A coherent outline for a research study that includes a potential research question, theoretical framework, and basic methodology (i.e., instrumentation).
rubrics: 2 outline possibilities for a research study that includes potential research question, theoretical framework, and basic methodology
Peer-reviewed academic sources or trade publications that justify and inform this outline

ratings.output_quality_reason: Overall, I”m pretty happy with today’s session, and I feel like this step is kind of the summary for it. I hit this stopping point fairly naturally towards the end of our session, and feel like I’ve got a pretty good working outline of a study idea that is taking shape and seems feasible.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: I took various bits and pieces from our conversation and typed them into a document that is how I’d like to outline the paper. I addressed most of the large-scale elements of a paper outline, particularly a theoretical framework and justification for asking/answering the research question. It needs WAY more work on the literature review and instrumentation, so that might be for a future session. However, it was a great start and I have a project outline that I’m happy with.
